title: Assessing the Feasibility of Collective Licensing of In-Copyright Works as Training Data for Generative AI Systems
pub: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, vol. 123 no. 30, e2509769122 (Law and AI Special Feature)
author: Pamela Samuelson

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: EU governance: Simplification tests enforceable safeguards
st.an: The excerpt is only a bibliography identifying the EU AI Act, copyright legislation, training-content transparency materials and commentary on the Brussels Effect. It provides no substantive findings, reasoning or recommendations from which to assess agreement with the cluster’s propositions on enforceable safeguards, regulatory design, implementation or cross-border convergence.
qs: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act) (“AI Act”).
European Commission, Explanatory Notice and Template for the Public Summary of Training Content for general-purpose AI models (24 July 2025).

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source addresses copyright licensing for AI training, creators’ interests, and broad societal effects rather than legal workflows, verification, competence, or lawyer replacement. Its qualified prediction of some job displacement and adaptation is too general to establish a position on the cluster’s legal-specific proposition.
qs: Generative AI may displace some opportunities and Sag and Yu suggest that countries are recognizing “that jobs, but society has adapted to many challenges arising from text and data mining, computational data analysis, and AI automation of previously human-skilled tasks and jobs.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source focuses on copyright licensing for AI training data, not task-level legal-AI capability, verification, user expertise or operating-model redesign. Its qualified observations about displacement, human authorship and policy risks are broadly compatible with the synthesis but insufficient to establish a position on its principal proposition.

kp.k: Collective licensing faces unresolved feasibility problems
kp.d: Samuelson assesses collective licensing as a proposed compromise between AI developers and copyright owners, rather than an established solution. Her perspective identifies normative, economic and practical obstacles affecting large developers, startups, research institutions and the public. The article concerns copyright regulation and AI development, not empirical changes to law-firm staffing or legal-service delivery.
qs: The feasibil- ity of such a system, and its possible ramifications, should be carefully considered before proceeding.

kp.k: Training litigation creates potentially severe development constraints
kp.d: The article reports more than four dozen lawsuits following the January 2023 Andersen action. Samuelson explains that successful fair-use defenses would permit continued exploitation and training, whereas copyright-owner victories could produce billions of dollars in damages, injunctions and even model destruction. These are conditional litigation consequences, not outcomes established across the cases.
qs: Fair use will be the main defense against these charges.

If fair use defenses succeed, developers will be free to continue to commercially exploit models already built on copyrighted data as well as to use these data to train new models or fine-tune existing ones.

kp.k: Fair-use arguments contest transformation and market harm
kp.d: Samuelson reports opposing litigant positions: plaintiffs emphasize commercial purposes, whole-work copying, competing outputs and lost licensing income; developers emphasize transformative data analysis, intermediate copying and prohibitive permission costs. She does not present either side's arguments as universally settled law.
qs: Second, training uses the works as data, not as works.
Third, the entirety of works in the dataset are copied in the training process, which disfavors fair use defenses.
There is consequently no cog- nizable harm to the plaintiffs’ markets.

kp.k: EU law distinguishes research privileges from commercial opt-outs
kp.d: The article explains that CDSMD Article 3 protects qualifying nonprofit scientific and cultural-heritage TDM on lawfully acquired copies, while Article 4 permits other TDM subject to right-holder opt-outs. AI Act Article 53 adds copyright-compliance policies and training-content summaries. These provisions are distinct from proposals to mandate collective licensing.
qs: In contrast, Article 7(1) of the CDSMD provides that any attempt to override the scientific and cultural heritage TDM privilege by contract will be unenforceable.
Neither the CDSMD nor the AI Act mentions collective licensing.

kp.k: EU extraterritorial copyright ambitions remain contested
kp.d: Samuelson interprets AI Act Recital 106 as seeking compliance with EU copyright standards even where models were trained elsewhere lawfully. She distinguishes that ambition from binding operative rules and notes debate over whether a recital can achieve this reach.
qs: Although recitals of EU regulations do not set forth binding rules, they may inform interpretations of the AI Act.
regardless of the jurisdiction in which the copyright-relevant acts underpinning the training of those general-purpose AI models take place.

kp.k: Opt-outs may favor incumbents over smaller participants
kp.d: Samuelson largely endorses European critics' prediction that large right-holders can use opt-outs to secure deals with large developers, while smaller creators may receive neither licensing offers nor compensation. Startups may be unable to negotiate comparable access. Individual authors may not benefit unless publishers are required to share revenues. These are distributional predictions, not measured market effects.
qs: The biggest disadvantage of the CDSMD opt-out approach is that it may produce a lose-lose situation.

Individual authors are unlikely to benefit from such deals unless the European Commission decides to impose an obligation on right-holders to share with authors some of the revenues they receive from AI model developers for training-data uses of their works.

kp.k: European proposals offer distinct remuneration mechanisms
kp.d: The article distinguishes voluntary CMO negotiations, Spain's proposed extended collective licensing covering nonmembers, and proposals to replace Article 4(3) with statutory remuneration. Geiger and Iaia favor access subject to payment; Frosio proposes compensation linked to empirically assessed disruption of creative markets, restricted to significantly affected creators and revisited over time. These remain proposals rather than adopted general AI licensing rules.
qs: Right-holders would need to opt-out of the CDSMD Article 4(1) TDM privilege to be eligible for compensation under the Spanish ECL proposal.
Yet, Frosio recommends that only those creators whose works are “sig- nificantly affected by AI could be entitled to these remuner- ations” (31, at 83).

kp.k: Commercialization levies defer payment but raise allocation questions
kp.d: Senftleben proposes allowing training without advance compensation and levying commercial AI products and services instead, with CMOs supporting human authorship. Samuelson identifies potential benefits for data access and entry barriers, but questions how recipients would be selected and revenues allocated. Quintais separately challenges the identification and calculation of compensable copyright harm.
qs: He proposes instead a levy on commercialization of generative AI products and ser- vices in the EU to support human authorship (22, at 1549).
if the copyright harm cannot be identified, how can we estab- lish the substitution effect of AI outputs on human-authored works?

kp.k: Fragmented rights infrastructure obstructs comprehensive licensing
kp.d: Samuelson describes EU clearance as fragmented across 27 member states, work categories and authorized uses. CMOs may lack authority over AI training, require costly acquisition of additional rights and lack copies of the works themselves. Existing blanket licenses therefore do not necessarily provide the coverage or content needed for large-scale model training.
qs: Each of the 27 EU member states has its own national copyright law, only some parts of which are harmo- nized across the Union.
Although CMOs may acquire rights, they generally do not have copies of works to license to AI developers.

kp.k: Input valuation and administration threaten meaningful creator payments
kp.d: Samuelson argues that contributions of particular training inputs cannot presently be valued, making equitable remuneration difficult. Given massive datasets and potentially millions of recipients, she predicts administration could absorb a large share of revenues. This is a feasibility argument, not an empirical estimate of eventual payout levels.
qs: At present, it is impossible to assess how much value particular inputs have contributed to models on which they were trained.
Yet details are sparse about how they would design a fair remuneration regime, and those details matter.

kp.k: US licensing advocates differ over compulsory arrangements
kp.d: The Authors Guild and eleven other creator organizations endorsed industry-by-industry voluntary collective licensing in August 2023, with an antitrust exemption to facilitate collaboration. AAP's Matthew Stratton argues licensing professional publishing and news content is feasible but opposes compulsory licensing. Sobel's earlier levy proposal acknowledges unresolved accounting and distribution problems and suggests charities or public creative-work programs if individual disbursement proves infeasible.
qs: The Guild wants collective licenses to be negotiated with AI model developers on an industry-by-industry basis, appropri- ate terms for which should be decided by each industry (39).
AAP will oppose any proposal that would call for compulsory licensing of copyrighted works as training data for generative AI models (40, at 448).

kp.k: Copyright Office favors developing voluntary licensing markets
kp.d: Samuelson reports that the Copyright Office's May 9, 2025 pre-publication report reached a use-specific fair-use conclusion and recommended allowing emerging voluntary licensing markets to develop. It favored voluntary licensing or, in some cases, ECL over compulsory licensing, while acknowledging challenges at scale. Its market analysis considered copying-based substitution, lost licenses and market dilution even without substantially similar outputs.
qs: Its overall conclusion was that some uses of works as training data may be fair, while others may be unfair (42, at 74).
It stated that where licensing was feasible, the market effects factor would cut against fair use.

kp.k: Bartz experts disputed training-license market feasibility
kp.d: Anthropic's expert Steven Peterson argued that dispersed rights, incomplete ownership information and transaction costs prevent a practicable large-scale text-licensing market; existing deals do not establish comprehensive feasibility. Plaintiffs' expert James E. Malackowski cited deals and willing licensors as evidence of an emerging book-training market. Samuelson notes his declaration was heavily redacted and did not discuss collective licensing; the court did not resolve these competing economic opinions.
qs: The “hypothetical market to license AI training data has none of the charac- teristics needed for it to function” (45, ¶49).
That this market is still emerging is not a reason to discount its plausibility (46, ¶50).
Malackowski’s declaration did not discuss collective licensing.

kp.k: Training fair use differs from pirated-book liability
kp.d: The article reports that the June 2025 Bartz ruling treated training uses as fair use. It separately records the September 5, 2025 announcement of a $1.5 billion settlement compensating right-holders for past downloading and storage of pirated books. The settlement is not presented as payment establishing infringement by training itself. Samuelson considers litigation-generated collective licensing possible but unlikely and constrained by courts' authority over litigants.
qs: The economists’ arguments did not play an important role in the eventual fair use ruling in the Bartz case.
On September 5, 2025, the litigants announced a settlement of $1.5 billion to compensate right-holders for Anthropic’s past acts of downloading and storing “pirated” books (44).

kp.k: US precedents reveal limited collective-licensing expansion
kp.d: Samuelson contrasts the limited US CMO infrastructure with Europe's and cites unsuccessful expansion efforts. The AHRA's last payout was only $56.43 in 2020; proposed peer-to-peer licensing failed to gain industry support and legislation; a mass-digitization ECL pilot encountered strong opposition. These historical examples support her skepticism without proving every future AI scheme must fail.
qs: Efforts to expand collective licensing in the United States have met with little success.
But the last payout from the AHRA fund was only $56.43 in 2020 (49).

kp.k: Uncertain ownership limits publishers' and CMOs' licensing authority
kp.d: Samuelson argues that older publishing contracts may not allocate unforeseen AI-training uses to publishers, requiring contract-specific examination. She invokes Rosetta Books' treatment of ebook rights and argues such unexpected rights should generally remain with authors. CCC's offerings cannot establish scalable clearance without valid mandates, while user-generated and open-source content further disperses ownership.
qs: If publishers are providing CCC with training-data rights, how can CCC be sure that the publishers actually own the rights?
In any event, one would have to examine the terms of book contracts to determine who might own what rights to license training-data uses of published books.

kp.k: Licensing feasibility depends on bounded versus unbounded training
kp.d: A February 2025 report by independent economists convened by the Copyright Office distinguished bounded models with identifiable works and owners, such as Adobe Firefly, from unbounded models using sources such as Common Crawl. It regarded licensing as feasible for the former but questioned the latter, emphasizing transaction costs and the difficulty of identifying individual inputs' contributions. Samuelson notes that the Office's subsequent pre-publication training report did not mention this economic report.
qs: The report observed that markets can fail if transaction costs outstrip the payments for right clearances (56, at 45–47).
It also emphasized the difficulty (and perhaps impossibility) of identifying the contribution of any one data source to the model’s performance

kp.k: Fair-use analysis should incorporate public benefits and creativity
kp.d: Samuelson recommends that courts apply Google v. Oracle's attention to public benefits and ongoing creativity, alongside possible copyright-owner harms. She argues that generative AI promotes consumer welfare and research participation, citing a 2024 study reporting nearly 40% US adult adoption for work or personal use. These broad adoption claims are not evidence of legal-profession-specific productivity effects.
qs: The development of generative AI technologies has pro- moted consumer welfare.

A 2024 study reported that nearly 40% of the U.S. adult population already uses generative AI for work or personal uses, across a broad range of occupations and tasks and at an adoption rate faster than PCs and the internet (59).

kp.k: Displacement and regulatory migration remain prospective concerns
kp.d: Samuelson acknowledges potential creative-job displacement and suggests taxation of AI products and services could offset some losses. She reports Sag and Yu's argument that an international consensus favoring training exceptions is emerging, citing Israel, Japan and Singapore, while describing China's possible permissive approach speculatively. She predicts restrictive national rules or cumulative licensing obligations could redirect investment and talent toward more favorable development environments.
qs: Revenues to off-set some job displacement can come about through taxing generative AI products and services.
The risk of regulatory arbitrage is real.
Countries with the least favorable copyright exceptions and development environments are unlikely to attract investment and talent.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Samuelson argues that copyright rules for AI training will shape AI development, market entry, creator compensation and public benefits; she doubts that collective licensing can resolve the training-data dilemma at general-purpose-model scale.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about copyright and generative-AI markets, not a prediction about law-firm staffing or legal-service delivery. Samuelson presents litigation outcomes conditionally: successful fair use defenses would permit continued exploitation and training, while copyright-owner victories could expose developers to substantial damages, injunctions and potentially model destruction. She predicts that EU opt-outs will primarily strengthen large right-holders' bargaining positions, while smaller right-holders and startups are less likely to secure comparable deals. She regards restrictions on access to European training works as likely to impair model development. Collective licensing faces fragmented rights ownership, uncertain training-rights mandates, territorial and sectoral divisions among collective management organizations, and potentially high administrative costs relative to individual payouts. She sees advantages in a commercialization levy over training-stage remuneration, but identifies unresolved questions about compensable harm and allocation. She also claims that generative AI promotes consumer welfare and innovation, may displace some creative opportunities and jobs, and can benefit authors themselves. She expects high-quality human authorship to remain valuable and warns that restrictive national rules can redirect AI investment and development toward more favorable jurisdictions. These are Samuelson's assessments; proposals she recounts from other scholars are not treated as her own predictions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source is a legal-policy perspective grounded in statutes, litigation, competing economic reports, licensing experience and secondary research, rather than original empirical measurement.
pts.d: Samuelson draws on U.S. fair use doctrine, EU copyright and AI legislation, and historical collective-licensing arrangements. She reports that the June 2025 Bartz ruling found the training uses fair without resolving the competing economists' assessments, and distinguishes that ruling from the September 2025 $1.5 billion settlement for past downloading and storage of pirated books. She describes Peterson's skepticism about scalable licensing and Malackowski's evidence of emerging licensing deals, rather than presenting either litigation expert's position as an established empirical result. Her skepticism also draws on a February 2025 independent economists' report commissioned by the Copyright Office, which distinguished bounded from unbounded models, and on unsuccessful or limited earlier licensing initiatives, including the AHRA's reported final payout of $56.43 in 2020. Existing publisher deals establish that some licensing occurs, but she disputes whether this demonstrates feasibility across internet-scale training data. Her consumer-adoption discussion cites a 2024 study reporting nearly 40% U.S. adult adoption, referenced through a working paper revised in February 2025; this supports adoption, not a measured causal estimate of welfare gains. Her predictions about entry barriers, migration, administrative burdens and creators' future prospects are principally analytical inferences supported by cited scholarship, not quantified forecasts.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most predictions are conditional on litigation, regulatory choices and licensing infrastructure, with no quantified forecast horizon.
pts.d: Although published in 2026, the article incorporates legal and policy developments through 2025 and describes a definitive U.S. resolution of training-data fair use as likely years away. The predicted damages and restrictions depend on copyright owners prevailing; continued training freedom depends on developers' fair use defenses succeeding. Licensing feasibility is qualified by model scope: bounded models with identifiable works and owners are distinguished from general-purpose models trained on massive, poorly documented internet corpora. Individual authors' benefits from large right-holder deals may depend on an obligation to share revenues. At the time described, the European Commission had not initiated a consultation on requiring collective licensing under Article 4. The possible extraterritorial effect of the AI Act is disputed, and Samuelson notes that its recitals are not themselves binding rules. She regards settlements seeding collective licensing as possible but unlikely. Predictions of relocation and reduced investment are contingent on differences among national copyright exceptions and development conditions; she supplies no schedule or numerical magnitude.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The distributional effects differ for large developers and right-holders, smaller entrants and creators, research institutions, and the public.
pts.d: Large commercial AI developers face copyright liability and licensing obligations but are better positioned than startups to negotiate major content deals. Large publishers and other right-holders gain bargaining power from opt-outs; individual authors may not share the resulting revenue, while small and medium-sized right-holders may be bypassed. Authors of open-source and user-generated content are especially difficult to incorporate into comprehensive licensing. Collective management organizations would face substantial rights-clearance, mandate, valuation and distribution tasks. Authors, artists and other creative workers face new competition and possible lost opportunities, but may also benefit from AI tools or policies supporting human creation. Universities and less-resourced researchers benefit from access to open models and weights. Consumers, enterprises, public bodies and research institutions benefit from access to AI tools, while restrictions on training or market entry may limit those benefits. Jurisdictions with unfavorable copyright and development environments risk losing investment and talent. The article does not separately measure effects on lawyers, law firms or legal-service clients.
